citation.title: De-homogenization using Convolutional Neural Networks
citation.authors: Martin O. Elingaard, Niels Aage, J. Andreas Bærentzen, Ole Sigmund
citation.venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The learned de-homogenization produces designs with compliance 7–25% from the homogenization-based reference while using a fraction of its computational cost.
claim.key_phrase: at a fraction of the computational cost
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Conclusion §5 states the method is 5 to 10 times faster than current de-homogenization approaches; 5 is the stated lower bound. Section 4.1 separately compares approximately 2.2 s with 16 s or 87 s per iteration and about 1,000 conventional iterations.
claim.alternatives: Section 4.1 estimates 5–10× less computational cost than prior de-homogenization; it also compares about 2.2 s projection with conventional topology optimization taking about 16 s or 87 s per iteration and roughly 1,000 iterations.

baseline.classical_method: Homogenization-based topology optimization followed by conventional least-squares de-homogenization; top88 SIMP used for the large-grid timing comparison (Section 4.1).
baseline.implementation: Prior de-homogenization least-squares method; top88 code for conventional topology optimization (Section 4.1).
baseline.hardware_classical: Modern-day laptop; specific model not stated (Section 4.1).
baseline.hardware_ml: Modern-day laptop; specific model not stated (Abstract; Section 4.1).
baseline.problem_size: 2400 × 1200 and 8000 × 2000 fine meshes; coarse input examples include 60 × 30 and 200 × 50 (Abstract; Section 4.1; Table 4).
baseline.classical_iterations: Continuation strategy typically around 1,000 iterations to converge for the top88 timing comparison (Section 4.1).
baseline.classical_time: top88: roughly 16 s and 87 s per iteration on 1440 × 720 and 2400 × 1200 meshes, respectively; roughly 16,000 s and 87,000 s for about 1,000 iterations (Section 4.1). Prior least-squares method: roughly 10 s for 1600 × 800 (Section 4.1).
baseline.ml_time: Approximately 1.3 s on 1440 × 720 and 2.2 s on 2400 × 1200 (Section 4.1).
baseline.training_time: Described as extremely inexpensive; no numeric training time stated (Conclusion §5).
baseline.data_generation_cost: Synthetic orientation-field data are used; generation cost not stated (Abstract; §3).
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance relative to homogenization-based reference; volume fraction and minimum relative thickness also considered (Abstract; Tables 1, 4, 5).
baseline.quality_gap: Abstract reports de-homogenized designs within 7–25% of the homogenization-based solution; double-clamped case averages 22.4% worse and violates volume constraint by 2.3% on average (Abstract; Table 4).

R1.evidence: Abstract; Section 4: the speed claim is accompanied by output quality 7–25% from the homogenization solution; no equal-quality or equal-time comparison is made.

R2.evidence: Section 4.1 reports the top88 comparison but does not establish that the classical baseline is inefficient under the protocol criteria.

R3.evidence: Sections 3 and 5: synthetic data and inexpensive training are described, but neither data-generation nor training cost is quantified and no break-even or per-query-only limitation is given.

R4.evidence: Section 4 and Tables 1, 4, 5 report compliance and volume results for designs; the article does not report a rate of disconnected or otherwise failed outputs.

reporting.n_test_cases: Several load and boundary-condition examples; 6 designs in the high-resolution timing summary (Abstract; Fig. 13).

notes: The paper notes that post-processing can overshoot the prescribed volume fraction and suggests subsequent finite-element checks as future work (§5).
